TERM_ANNASAMANA: Aññasamāna cetasikas are the 13 'ethically variable' mental factors — the 7 universals and 6 occasionals — that take on a wholesome, unwholesome or indeterminate character depending on the citta they accompany.
TERM_SABBACITTA: The seven universal mental factors (Sabbacittasādhāraṇa) arise in absolutely every citta without exception, providing the basic structure of any act of cognition.
TERM_PAKINNAKA: The six occasional mental factors (Pakiṇṇaka) arise only in certain cittas, not in all of them, unlike the seven universals.
TERM_PHASSA_M1: Contact (Phassa) is the mental factor that brings sense base, object and consciousness together, the condition for feeling to arise.
TERM_VEDANA_M1: Feeling (Vedanā) is the mental factor that experiences the affective quality — pleasant, painful or neutral — of an object.
TERM_SANNA_M1: Perception (Saññā) is the mental factor that marks and recognises an object by its distinguishing features, allowing it to be remembered later.
TERM_CETANA_M1: Volition (Cetanā) is the mental factor of intention that organises the other co-arisen factors toward the object and is what actually creates kamma.
TERM_EKAGGATA_M1: One-pointedness (Ekaggatā) is the mental factor that unifies citta and its associated factors onto a single object, the seed of concentration.
TERM_JIVITINDRIYA_M1: The life faculty (Jīvitindriya) is the mental factor that maintains and vitalises its co-arisen mental phenomena for the duration of a mind-moment.
TERM_MANASIKARA_M1: Attention (Manasikāra) is the mental factor that turns citta and its associated factors toward the object, like a rudder steering a boat.
TERM_PAKINNAKA_M11: The six occasional mental factors (Pakiṇṇaka) arise only in certain cittas, not in all of them, unlike the seven universals.
TERM_ANNASAMANA_M11: Aññasamāna cetasikas are the 13 ethically variable mental factors — 7 universal and 6 occasional — that take on the ethical colour of whatever citta they accompany.
TERM_VITAKKA: Initial application (Vitakka) is the mental factor that lifts citta and its associated factors onto the object for the first time, like a bee flying toward a flower.
TERM_VICARA: Sustained application (Vicāra) is the mental factor that keeps the mind anchored on and examining the object continuously, like a bee circling the flower it has landed on.
TERM_ADHIMOKKHA: Decision (Adhimokkha) is the mental factor that resolves the mind firmly upon its object, releasing it from wavering and doubt.
TERM_VIRIYA: Energy (Vīriya) is the mental factor of effort that supports and sustains its co-arisen states so they do not fall back from their task.
TERM_SAMMAPADHANA: The Four Right Strivings (Sammāpadhāna) are the fourfold application of energy: to prevent, abandon, develop and maintain, directed at unwholesome and wholesome states.
TERM_PITI: Rapture (Pīti) is the mental factor of joyful interest in the object, ranging from a slight thrill to a rapture that pervades the whole body.
TERM_CHANDA: Desire-to-act (Chanda) is the simple wish to do or to obtain, ethically neutral in itself until it is qualified by the citta it occurs in.
TERM_AKUSALA_CET: An unwholesome mental factor (akusala cetasika) is a mental factor that occurs only in unwholesome consciousness, rooted in greed, hatred or delusion.
TERM_MOCATUKA: The delusion group (Mocatuka) comprises the four mental factors — delusion, shamelessness, fearlessness of wrongdoing and restlessness — that accompany every unwholesome citta without exception.
TERM_AHIRIKA: Shamelessness (Ahirika) is the absence of moral shame, the mental factor that feels no disgust toward committing an unwholesome deed.
TERM_ANOTTAPPA: Fearlessness of wrongdoing (Anottappa) is the absence of moral dread, the mental factor that feels no fear of the consequences of an unwholesome deed.
TERM_UDDHACCA: Restlessness (Uddhacca) is the mental factor of agitation that prevents the mind from settling calmly on its object.
TERM_CITTA_M4: Citta is the basic unit of consciousness — the faculty that cognises an object, arising and perishing together with its associated mental factors in a single mind-moment.
TERM_AKUSALACITTA: An unwholesome citta (akusala citta) is a moment of consciousness rooted in greed, hatred or delusion, productive of a painful result.
TERM_LOBHA_M4: Greed (Lobha) is the mental factor that clings to and grasps at an agreeable object, the root of the eight greed-rooted unwholesome cittas.
TERM_ASANKHARIKA: Unprompted (Asaṅkhārika) describes a citta that arises spontaneously, of its own accord, without external or internal inducement.
TERM_SASANKHARIKA: Prompted (Sasaṅkhārika) describes a citta that arises only after inducement — one's own deliberation or another person's urging.
TERM_DITTHIGATA: Associated with wrong view (Diṭṭhigatasampayutta) describes a greed-rooted citta that is accompanied by a mistaken view, such as belief in a permanent self.
TERM_DOSA_M4: Hatred (Dosa) is the mental factor of aversion that reacts against a disagreeable object, the root shared by the two hatred-rooted unwholesome cittas.
TERM_PATIGHA: Repulsion (Paṭigha) is the striking, harsh quality of the mind when it collides with an unwanted object — a synonym closely linked to hatred.
TERM_DOMANASSA: Painful mental feeling (Domanassa) is the unpleasant affective tone that necessarily accompanies every hatred-rooted citta.
TERM_MOHA_M4: Delusion (Moha) is the mental factor of fundamental unknowing that obscures the true nature of phenomena and is present in every unwholesome citta.
TERM_VICIKICCHA: Doubt (Vicikicchā) is the mental factor of sceptical indecision about the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Sangha, and the nature of kamma.
TERM_AYONISO: Unwise attention (Ayoniso manasikāra) is attention that engages an object in a way that is not conducive to seeing it correctly — the proximate cause of delusion.
TERM_AKUSALA_NGU_M4: Akusala has five traditional meanings: diseased, unlovely, unskilful, productive of suffering, and the opposite of what is wholesome.
TERM_LOBHA_NHOM_M4: The greed group (lobhatuka cetasika) comprises greed, wrong view and conceit, the three mental factors specific to the eight greed-rooted cittas.
TERM_DOSA_NHOM_M4: The hatred group (dosatuka cetasika) comprises hatred, envy, avarice and worry, the four mental factors specific to the two hatred-rooted cittas.
TERM_LOBHA_DIṬṬHI_M4: Greed (Lobha) is the root mental factor of attachment that clings to an agreeable object; it is present in all eight greed-rooted cittas.
TERM_DITTHI_M4: Wrong view (Diṭṭhi) is the mental factor that misapprehends the nature of phenomena, most commonly by assuming a permanent self or a wrong account of kamma.
TERM_SAKKAYA_M4: Personality view (Sakkāyadiṭṭhi) is the specific wrong view that takes the five aggregates, or part of them, to be a self or to belong to a self; it is eradicated at stream-entry.
TERM_MANA_M4: Conceit (Māna) is the mental factor of self-comparison — measuring oneself as better, equal or worse than others — distinct from wrong view though both involve the sense of 'I'.
TERM_DOSA_NHOM_SAN_M4: Hatred (Dosa) is the root mental factor of aversion present in both hatred-rooted cittas and shared by envy, avarice and worry.
TERM_ISSA_M4: Envy (Issā) is the mental factor that cannot bear another's success or good fortune.
TERM_MACCHARIYA_M4: Avarice (Macchariya) is the mental factor that cannot bear to share one's own gains, praise or good fortune with others.
TERM_KUKKUCCA_M4: Worry (Kukkucca) is the mental factor of regret over wholesome deeds left undone or unwholesome deeds already done.
TERM_THINA_M4: Sloth (Thīna) is the mental factor of sickness or stiffness of the citta itself — a lack of readiness and energy in the mind.
TERM_MIDDHA_M4: Torpor (Middha) is the mental factor of sickness or stiffness in the associated mental factors — drowsiness and unwieldiness of the mental body.
TERM_THINA_MIDDHA_M4: Sloth and torpor (Thīna-Middha) always arise together as a pair, and only in prompted unwholesome cittas, since the lack of readiness they denote requires some inducement to override.
TERM_VICIKICCHA_M4: Doubt (Vicikicchā) is the mental factor of sceptical indecision that cannot settle on the truth of the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Sangha, the training, or dependent origination.
TERM_AHETUKA: Rootless (Ahetuka) describes a citta that arises without any of the six roots (greed, hatred, delusion, non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion), and so is ethically weak, incapable of great wholesome or unwholesome force.
TERM_NHAN_DI_THOI: 'Nānākālika hetu' denotes a root that conditions its associated states by way of a different-time relationship, explaining how a rootless resultant citta can still trace its origin to a rooted kamma performed earlier.
TERM_AKUSALA_VIPAKA_M12: Unwholesome-resultant rootless consciousness (akusala-vipāka ahetuka) comprises the seven rootless cittas that are the direct results of past unwholesome kamma, each experiencing an undesirable object.
TERM_KUSALA_VIPAKA_M12: Wholesome-resultant rootless consciousness (kusala-vipāka ahetuka) comprises the eight rootless cittas that are the direct results of past wholesome kamma, each experiencing a desirable object.
TERM_AVJJANA: Adverting (Āvajjana) is the function of turning the mind toward an object as a cognitive process begins; it is rootless and creates no kamma.
TERM_HASITUPPADA: Smile-producing consciousness (Hasituppāda) is the rootless functional citta unique to Arahants, responsible for their smile at ordinary sense objects.
TERM_SOBHANA: Beautiful (Sobhana) describes cittas and cetasikas that are pure, skilful and radiant, encompassing wholesome, wholesome-resultant and functional beautiful consciousness.
TERM_VIRATI: The abstinences (Viratiyo) are the three mental factors — right speech, right action and right livelihood — that consciously refrain from unwholesome bodily and verbal conduct.
TERM_SADDHA_M3: Faith (Saddhā) is the mental factor that clarifies and settles the mind with confidence in worthy objects such as the Triple Gem and the law of kamma.
TERM_SATI_M3: Mindfulness (Sati) is the mental factor that keeps the object in view without floating away, like a gatekeeper who does not let in what should not enter.
TERM_HIRI_M3: Moral shame (Hiri) is the mental factor that recoils from unwholesome conduct out of inner self-respect.
TERM_OTTAPPA_M3: Moral dread (Ottappa) is the mental factor that recoils from unwholesome conduct out of fear of its consequences and respect for others.
TERM_TATRAMAJJHATTATA_M3: Equanimity (Tatramajjhattatā) is the mental factor of mental balance that keeps citta and its associated factors evenly poised, neither too excited nor too depressed.
TERM_APPAMANNA: The illimitables (Appamaññā) are compassion and appreciative joy, called 'immeasurable' because they extend toward all beings without restriction of number.
TERM_MUDITA_M3: Appreciative joy (Muditā) is the mental factor that rejoices in the success and good fortune of others, opposed to envy.
TERM_PANNINDRIYA: The wisdom faculty (Paññindriya) is the mental factor of wisdom that understands things according to their true nature; it is the controlling faculty of insight.
TERM_SAMMAVACA_M3: Right speech (Sammāvācā) is the abstinence that refrains from lying, slander, harsh speech and idle chatter.
TERM_SAMMAKAMMANTA_M3: Right action (Sammākammanto) is the abstinence that refrains from killing, stealing and sexual misconduct.
TERM_SAMMAAJIVA_M3: Right livelihood (Sammā-ājīvo) is the abstinence that refrains from earning one's living by wrong speech or wrong action.
TERM_SAMMASADDHA_M3: Right faith (Sammāsaddhā) is confidence correctly placed in the Triple Gem and the law of kamma, as opposed to blind or misplaced faith.
TERM_ALOBHA_M3: Non-greed (Alobha) is the mental factor of detachment and generosity, one of the three wholesome roots, opposed to greed.
TERM_ADOSA_M3: Non-hatred (Adosa) is the mental factor of loving-kindness and good will, one of the three wholesome roots, opposed to hatred.
TERM_KAYA_CITTA_M3: 'Kāya-Citta' designates six pairs of beautiful mental factors that occur in parallel forms for the mental body and for consciousness itself: tranquillity, lightness, pliancy, wieldiness, proficiency and rectitude.
TERM_PASSADDHI_M3: Tranquillity (Passaddhi) is the mental factor that calms the agitation of the mental body and of consciousness.
TERM_LAHUTA_M3: Lightness (Lahutā) is the mental factor of buoyancy in the mental body and in consciousness, the opposite of heaviness and sluggishness.
TERM_MUDUTA_M3: Pliancy (Mudutā) is the mental factor of softness and adaptability in the mental body and in consciousness, the opposite of rigidity.
TERM_KAMMANNATA_M3: Wieldiness (Kammaññatā) is the mental factor of workability in the mental body and in consciousness, making them fit for wholesome action.
TERM_PAGUNNATA_M3: Proficiency (Pāguññatā) is the mental factor of skill and firmness in the mental body and in consciousness, free from sickness.
TERM_UJUKATA_M3: Rectitude (Ujukatā) is the mental factor of straightness in the mental body and in consciousness, free from the crookedness of deceit and hypocrisy.
TERM_TAM_TUE_M3: Wisdom arises in three stages — learning (Suttamayā), reflection (Cintāmayā) and mental development (Bhāvanāmayā) — knowledge gained respectively by study, by reasoning, and by direct meditative insight.
TERM_TU_QUYEN_M3: The wisdom faculty (Paññindriya) is the mental factor of wisdom that understands things according to their true nature; it is the controlling faculty of insight.
TERM_MAHAKUSALA: A great wholesome citta (Mahākusala citta) is one of the eight sense-sphere wholesome consciousnesses that create kamma leading to a pleasant rebirth or result.
TERM_MAHAVIPAKA: A great resultant citta (Mahāvipāka citta) is one of the eight sense-sphere resultant consciousnesses produced by great wholesome kamma, functioning as rebirth-linking, life-continuum, death or registering consciousness.
TERM_MAHAKIRIYA: A great functional citta (Mahākiriya citta) is one of the eight sense-sphere functional consciousnesses that occur only in Arahants, performing mental activity without creating kamma.
TERM_NANASAMPAYUTTA: Associated with knowledge (Ñāṇasampayutta) describes a citta that is accompanied by wisdom, understanding the true nature of the object.
TERM_NANAVIPPAYUTTA: Dissociated from knowledge (Ñāṇavippayutta) describes a citta that lacks the accompaniment of wisdom, though it may still be wholesome.
TERM_KAMAVACARA_M5: Sense-sphere (Kāmāvacara) describes consciousness that frequents the realm of sense-desire, as opposed to consciousness bound to the fine-material or immaterial jhānas.
TERM_MAHAGGATA: Exalted (Mahaggata) describes the fine-material and immaterial sphere cittas, so called because they are developed to a lofty degree through jhāna, overcoming the limitations of sense-sphere consciousness.
TERM_RUPAVACARA: Fine-material-sphere (Rūpāvacara) describes consciousness that frequents the realm attained through the fine-material jhānas.
TERM_JHANA_M13: Jhāna is the state of meditative absorption in which the mind is firmly fixed on a single object through the jhāna factors, temporarily suppressing the five hindrances.
TERM_EKAGGATA_M13: One-pointedness (Ekaggatā) is the jhāna factor of unification that becomes the dominant factor of absorption from the second jhāna onward, once initial and sustained application have been abandoned.
TERM_ABHINNA: The supernormal powers (Abhiññā) are direct knowledges — such as the divine eye and divine ear — attainable through mastery of the fifth fine-material jhāna.
TERM_NIRODHA: The attainment of cessation (Nirodha-samāpatti) is a state, accessible only to non-returners and Arahants who have mastered all eight jhānas, in which consciousness and mental factors temporarily cease altogether.
TERM_ARUPAVACARA: Immaterial-sphere (Arūpāvacara) describes consciousness that frequents the four formless attainments, transcending even subtle materiality as an object.
TERM_AYATANA_M14: A base (Āyatana) here denotes one of the four immaterial attainments, each named after the subtle object on which that jhāna is based.
TERM_AKASANANCAYATANA: The base of boundless space (Ākāsānañcāyatana) is the first immaterial jhāna, attained by taking the concept of infinite space, left after the removal of a kasiṇa sign, as its object.
TERM_VINNANANCAYATANA: The base of boundless consciousness (Viññāṇañcāyatana) is the second immaterial jhāna, attained by taking the consciousness that pervaded the base of boundless space as its object.
TERM_AKINCANNAYATANA: The base of nothingness (Ākiñcaññāyatana) is the third immaterial jhāna, attained by focusing on the total absence of the consciousness of boundless space.
TERM_NEVASANNANASANNAYATANA: The base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (Nevasaññā-nāsaññāyatana) is the fourth and subtlest immaterial jhāna, in which perception is so attenuated it can be called neither present nor absent.
TERM_ARUPA_KIRIYA: Immaterial-sphere functional consciousness (Arūpāvacara-kiriyā) comprises the four functional jhāna attainments experienced only by Arahants who have mastered the formless jhānas.
TERM_LOKUTTARA: Supramundane (Lokuttara) describes the path and fruition cittas and Nibbāna, which transcend the three mundane realms of existence altogether.
TERM_MAGGACITTA: A path citta (Magga citta) is a supramundane consciousness that arises only once in a lifetime at one of the four stages of awakening, directly eradicating defilements.
TERM_PHALACITTA: A fruition citta (Phala citta) is the supramundane resultant consciousness that immediately follows its corresponding path citta and may recur afterwards as the attainment of fruition.
TERM_SOTAPATTI: Stream-entry (Sotāpatti) is the first stage of awakening, at which personality view, doubt and attachment to rites and rituals are permanently eradicated.
TERM_SAKADAGAMI: Once-returning (Sakadāgāmi) is the second stage of awakening, at which gross sensual desire and ill will are attenuated though not yet eradicated.
TERM_ANAGAMI: Non-returning (Anāgāmi) is the third stage of awakening, at which sensual desire and ill will are permanently eradicated.
TERM_ARAHATTA: Arahantship (Arahatta) is the fourth and final stage of awakening, at which all remaining defilements are eradicated and no further rebirth occurs.
TERM_SAKKAYADITTHI: Personality view (Sakkāyadiṭṭhi) is the wrong view that takes the five aggregates to constitute or contain a permanent self; it is among the first three fetters eradicated at stream-entry.
TERM_SILABBATA: Attachment to rites and rituals (Sīlabbataparāmāsa) is the fetter of believing that ritual observance alone, apart from the Noble Eightfold Path, can lead to liberation; it is eradicated at stream-entry.
TERM_KAMMA: Kamma is volitional action — the mental factor of volition (cetanā) expressed through body, speech or mind — that produces a corresponding result.
TERM_CETANA: Volition (Cetanā) is the mental factor of intention that constitutes kamma itself, organising associated states toward an action and determining its ethical quality.
TERM_KAYAKAMMA: Bodily kamma (Kāyakamma) is volition expressed through bodily action, such as killing, stealing or sexual misconduct.
TERM_VACIKAMMA: Verbal kamma (Vacīkamma) is volition expressed through speech, such as lying, slander, harsh speech or idle chatter.
TERM_MANOKAMMA: Mental kamma (Manokamma) is volition that remains purely at the level of thought, such as covetousness, ill will or wrong view.
TERM_KAMMACATUKKA: The fourfold analysis of kamma (Kammacatukka) classifies kamma in four complementary ways: by function, by priority of ripening, by time of ripening, and by plane of ripening.
TERM_JANAKA: Generative kamma (Janakakamma) is the kamma that produces the resultant aggregates at rebirth and continues to produce mind-born materiality throughout life.
TERM_UPATTHAMBHAKA: Supportive kamma (Upatthambhakakamma) is kamma that generates no new result of its own but strengthens and extends a result that another kamma has already produced.
TERM_UPAPILAKA: Obstructive kamma (Upapīḷakakamma) is kamma that weakens or obstructs the result of another kamma that is already ripening.
TERM_UPAGHATAKA: Destructive kamma (Upaghātakakamma) is an especially powerful kamma that cuts off another kamma's result entirely and substitutes its own.
TERM_PATISANDHI: Rebirth-linking consciousness (Paṭisandhi viññāṇa) is the first moment of a new existence, generated by generative kamma, that links one life to the next.
TERM_GARUKA: Weighty kamma (Garukakamma) is kamma so powerful — either the jhānas or the five heinous deeds — that it is certain to produce rebirth and can never become defunct.
TERM_ANANTARIYA: The five heinous deeds (Ānantariyakamma) — matricide, patricide, killing an Arahant, wounding a Buddha, and causing a schism in the Sangha — are weighty unwholesome kammas that bring immediate rebirth in hell.
TERM_ASANNA: Death-proximate kamma (Āsannakamma) is the kamma, or the mental image associated with it, recollected or appearing just before death, determining rebirth in the absence of weighty kamma.
TERM_ACINNA: Habitual kamma (Āciṇṇakamma) is kamma performed repeatedly as a habit, gaining strength through constant repetition.
TERM_KATATTA: Reserve kamma (Kaṭattākamma) is the residue of all other actions performed, too weak to be weighty, death-proximate or habitual, yet available to produce rebirth if nothing stronger intervenes.
TERM_JAVANA: Impulsion (Javana) is the stage of a cognitive process, usually seven mind-moments long, in which kamma is actually created.
TERM_DITTHADHAMMA: Immediately-effective kamma (Diṭṭhadhammavedanīyakamma) is kamma that can ripen only within the same life in which it was performed, or else becomes defunct.
TERM_UPAPAJJA: Subsequently-effective kamma (Upapajjavedanīyakamma) is kamma that can ripen only in the life immediately following, or else becomes defunct.
TERM_APARAPARIYA: Indefinitely-effective kamma (Aparāpariyavedanīyakamma) is kamma that can ripen at any time from the third life onward until final liberation, without expiring.
TERM_AHOSI: Defunct kamma (Ahosikamma) is kamma that has lost its opportunity to ripen within its allotted time and so can no longer produce a result.
TERM_KAMAVACARA_K: Sense-sphere wholesome kamma (Kāmāvacarakusala) is wholesome kamma performed through the eight great wholesome cittas, ripening as happiness within the sense sphere.
TERM_RUPAVACARA_K: Fine-material-sphere wholesome kamma (Rūpāvacarakusala) is the kamma of the five fine-material jhānas, ripening as rebirth in the corresponding Brahmā realm.
TERM_ARUPAVACARA_K: Immaterial-sphere wholesome kamma (Arūpāvacarakusala) is the kamma of the four formless jhānas, ripening as rebirth in the corresponding formless realm.
TERM_PANATIPATA: Killing living beings (Pāṇātipāta) is one of the ten unwholesome courses of action, performed through the body.
TERM_MUSAVADA: False speech (Musāvāda) is one of the ten unwholesome courses of action, performed through speech.
TERM_ABHIJJHA: Covetousness (Abhijjhā) is one of the ten unwholesome courses of action, performed purely through the mind, longing for another's possessions.
TERM_SAMMADITTHI: Right view (Sammādiṭṭhi) is one of the ten wholesome courses of action, performed through the mind, understanding kamma and its results correctly.
TERM_TIHETUKA: Triple-rooted (Tihetuka) describes a wholesome or unwholesome citta, or a being born from such kamma, possessing all three of its appropriate roots, giving it full ethical and cognitive strength.
TERM_DVIHETUKA: Double-rooted (Dvihetuka) describes a citta, or a being born from such kamma, possessing only two of the three roots, typically lacking non-delusion (wisdom).
TERM_KAMMAJA_RUPA: Kamma-born materiality (Kammaja-rūpa) is physical matter produced directly by past kamma, present from the moment of rebirth-linking and continuously throughout life.
TERM_PATICCA: Dependent origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda) is the twelvefold chain of conditions through which ignorance leads, link by link, to ageing and death, explaining the round of rebirth without needing a permanent self.
TERM_PATTHANA: The Conditional Relations (Paṭṭhāna) is the seventh and final book of the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, analysing the twenty-four modes of conditionality (paccaya) that underlie dependent origination.
TERM_PACCAYA: A condition (Paccaya) is a phenomenon on which another phenomenon depends for its arising, persistence or particular nature.
TERM_AVIJJA: Ignorance (Avijjā) is not knowing the Four Noble Truths, kamma and its result, and dependent origination itself — the first link of the twelvefold chain.
TERM_SANKHARA: Formations (Saṅkhārā) are the volitional activities — kamma — conditioned by ignorance, which in turn condition the arising of rebirth-consciousness.
TERM_VINNANA: Consciousness (Viññāṇa) here denotes rebirth-linking consciousness, conditioned by formations (kamma) and in turn conditioning mind-and-matter in the new existence.
TERM_NAMARUPA: Mind-and-matter (Nāmarūpa) are the mental and material aggregates that develop together, conditioned by rebirth consciousness, forming the basis for the six sense bases.
TERM_SALAYATANA: The six sense bases (Saḷāyatana) — eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind — develop from mind-and-matter and provide the doors through which contact occurs.
TERM_JARAMARANA: Ageing-and-death (Jarāmaraṇa) is the final link, the inevitable decay and dissolution of whatever has been born, bringing a fresh round of suffering unless the chain is broken.
TERM_TAYO_ADDHA: The three periods (Tayo addhā) divide the twelve links across past, present and future lives: two links in the past, eight in the present, two in the future.
TERM_VISATAKARA: The twenty modes (Vīsatākārā) break the twelve links down into five past causes, five present results, five present causes and five future results.
TERM_TISANDHI: The three connections (Tisandhi) are the junctions linking past causes to present results, present results to present causes, and present causes to future results.
TERM_CATUSANKHEPA: The four groupings (Catusaṅkhepa) summarise the twelve links into four compact categories: past causes, present results, present causes and future results.
TERM_KILESAVATTA: The round of defilements (Kilesavaṭṭa) comprises ignorance, craving and clinging — the links that generate new kamma.
TERM_KAMMAVATTA: The round of kamma (Kammavaṭṭa) comprises formations and the kamma-process portion of becoming — the links that actively produce future results.
TERM_VIPAKAVATTA: The round of results (Vipākavaṭṭa) comprises consciousness, mind-and-matter, the six bases, contact and feeling — the links that are passively experienced as results.
TERM_DVE_MULANI: The two roots (Dve mūlāni) of the round of rebirth are ignorance, rooted in the past, and craving, rooted in the present — cutting either breaks the cycle.
TERM_APUNNA: Demeritorious formations (Apuññābhisaṅkhāra) are the volitional formations of the twelve unwholesome cittas, producing an unhappy rebirth.
TERM_PUNNA: Meritorious formations (Puññābhisaṅkhāra) are the volitional formations of sense-sphere and fine-material-sphere wholesome cittas, producing a happy rebirth.
TERM_ANENJA: Imperturbable formations (Āneñjābhisaṅkhāra) are the volitional formations of the four immaterial-sphere wholesome cittas, so called because they are unshaken by the sense-sphere hindrances.
TERM_RUPA: Materiality (Rūpa) is physical phenomena, analysed in the Abhidhamma into 28 types grouped under the four great elements and the matter derived from them.
TERM_AHETUKA_R: Rootless (Ahetuka), applied to materiality, indicates that matter is never directly accompanied by the six roots the way mental states are — the roots condition it only indirectly, through kamma.
TERM_ANARAMMANA: Objectless (Anārammaṇa) describes matter's inability to cognise anything — unlike citta and cetasika, materiality never takes an object.
TERM_MAHABHUTA: The four great elements (Mahābhūtāni) — earth, water, fire and air — are the primary types of matter on which all other, derived materiality depends.
TERM_UPADAYA: Derived materiality (Upādāyarūpāni) comprises the 24 types of matter, such as the sense organs and sense objects, that arise dependent on the four great elements.
TERM_PATHAVI: The earth element (Paṭhavī-dhātu) is the element of extension and solidity, experienced as hardness or softness.
TERM_APO: The water element (Āpo-dhātu) is the element of cohesion and fluidity, which binds other material particles together; it cannot be directly touched.
TERM_TEJO: The fire element (Tejo-dhātu) is the element of temperature, experienced as heat or cold.
TERM_VAYO: The air element (Vāyo-dhātu) is the element of motion and pressure, experienced as tactile distension or support.
TERM_PASADA: Sensitive matter (Pasādarūpa) comprises the five sense organs — eye, ear, nose, tongue and body — the physical bases sensitive to their respective objects.
TERM_GOCARA: Sense-field matter (Gocararūpa) comprises the objects of the five senses — visible form, sound, odour, taste and the tangible elements.
TERM_HADAYA: The heart-base (Hadayavatthu) is the material support for mind-element and mind-consciousness-element, the physical basis of mental activity apart from the five sense doors.
TERM_VINNATTI: Intimation (Viññattirūpa) is bodily and vocal expression — gesture and speech — through which an intention is communicated to others.
TERM_LAKKHANA: The characteristics of matter (Lakkhaṇarūpa) are the four phases common to all conditioned matter: production, continuity, decay and impermanence.
TERM_NIPPHANNA: Concretely-produced matter (Nipphannarūpa) is the 18 types of real, directly-conditioned materiality — such as the elements and sense organs — suitable for insight contemplation.
TERM_ANIPPHANNA: Non-concretely-produced matter (Anipphannarūpa) is the 10 types of matter, such as space and the characteristics of matter, that are modes or boundaries of real matter rather than realities in their own right.
TERM_SAMUTTHANA: The origination of matter (Rūpasamuṭṭhāna) refers to the four sources from which material phenomena arise: kamma, consciousness, temperature and nutriment.
TERM_UTU: Temperature (Utu) is one of the four originators of matter, the fire element present in a preceding group of matter that generates new matter both in the body and in the external world.
TERM_OJA: Nutritive essence (Ojā / Āhāra) is one of the four originators of matter, the nutritive factor in food that, once digested, generates new matter throughout the body.
TERM_CITTAVITHI: A cognitive process (Cittavīthi) is the structured sequence of cittas, each performing a specific function, that cognises a single object from its appearance through to its fading from the mind.
TERM_DVARA: A door (Dvāra) is one of the six channels — the five physical sense doors plus the mind-door — through which an object can enter a cognitive process.
TERM_VATTHU: A physical base (Vatthu) is the material support on which a citta depends to arise, such as the eye-base for eye-consciousness or the heart-base for mind-consciousness.
TERM_ATIMAHANTA: A very great object (Atimahanta-ārammaṇa) is a sense object that strikes its sense base with enough force to generate the full seventeen mind-moments of a complete cognitive process, including registration.
TERM_VIBHUTA: A clear object (Vibhūta-ārammaṇa) is a mind-door object strong enough to run through impulsion but not strong enough to produce registration afterwards.
TERM_BHAVANGA: The life-continuum (Bhavaṅga) is the resultant consciousness that flows between cognitive processes, maintaining the unbroken continuity of a being's mental stream.
TERM_PANCADVARA: Five-door adverting (Pañcadvārāvajjana) is the functional citta that opens one of the five sense doors and turns attention toward an arriving object, beginning a sense-door cognitive process.
TERM_SAMPATICCHANA: Receiving consciousness (Sampaṭicchana) is the rootless resultant citta that receives a sense object immediately after the corresponding sense consciousness has known it.
TERM_SANTIRANA: Investigating consciousness (Santīraṇa) is the rootless resultant citta that examines an object received from the senses to determine whether it is desirable or not.
TERM_VOTTHAPANA: Determining consciousness (Voṭṭhapana) is the functional citta that makes the final determination of an object as good or bad, opening the way for the impulsions that follow.
TERM_TADALAMBANA: Registration (Tadālambana) is the resultant consciousness that arises for two mind-moments after impulsion, when the object is clear enough, continuing to experience the residual object.
TERM_JAVANA_M10: Impulsion (Javana) is the stage of a cognitive process, usually seven consecutive mind-moments, in which the citta actually experiences the object fully and creates kamma.
TERM_BIJAKAMMA: 'Seed kamma' (Bījakamma) describes how, among the seven impulsion moments, the first and last create comparatively weak kamma while the middle five create the kamma most likely to determine the next rebirth.
TERM_TADALAMBANA_2: Registration (Tadālambana) is the resultant consciousness that arises for two mind-moments after impulsion, when the object is clear enough, continuing to experience the residual object.
TERM_MANODVARA: The mind-door process (Manodvāra-vīthi) is a cognitive process that cognises a mind-object directly through the mind door, without passing through any of the five physical senses, as in thinking, remembering or imagining.
TERM_MANODVARAVAJJANA: Mind-door adverting (Manodvārāvajjana) is the functional citta that turns attention to a mind-door object and, uniquely, also performs the determining function in a five-door process.
TERM_VITHIMUTTA: Process-freed consciousness (Vīthimutta) comprises the cittas that operate outside any cognitive process — rebirth-linking, life-continuum and death consciousness.
TERM_CETASIKASANGAHA_M15: The compendium of mental factors (Cetasikasaṅgaha) is the Abhidhamma analysis that cross-tabulates all 52 cetasikas against the 89/121 cittas, showing exactly which factors associate with which types of consciousness.
TERM_TO_THA_13_M15: Aññasamāna cetasikas are the 13 ethically variable mental factors — 7 universal and 6 occasional — that take on the ethical colour of whatever citta they accompany.
TERM_BAT_THIEN_BIEN_HANH_M15: The unwholesome universals (Akusalasādhāraṇā) are the four mental factors — delusion, shamelessness, fearlessness of wrongdoing and restlessness — present in every one of the twelve unwholesome cittas.
TERM_TONG_SO_TS_M15: A numeric total within the combination tables, marking a count rather than a named technical term.
TERM_PARAMATTHA_M15: Ultimate reality (Paramatthasacca) comprises the four irreducible realities recognised by the Abhidhamma — citta, cetasika, rūpa and Nibbāna — as opposed to the conventional realities of ordinary language.
TERM_TU_DANH_UAN_M15: The mental aggregates (Nāma-khandha) are feeling, perception, formations and consciousness — the four non-material aggregates that, together with the aggregate of matter, exhaustively classify all experience.
TERM_THAM_19_21_M15: Greed-rooted cittas (Lobhamūla) are the eight unwholesome consciousnesses rooted in greed, among the standard list of 89/121 cittas.
TERM_SAN_20_22_M15: Hatred-rooted cittas (Dosamūla) are the two unwholesome consciousnesses rooted in hatred.
TERM_NGU_song_THUC_M15: The ten sense-consciousnesses (Dvipañcaviññāṇa) are the five pairs of eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue- and body-consciousness, each occurring as an unwholesome-resultant and a wholesome-resultant citta.
TERM_VI_TIEU_M15: Smile-producing consciousness (Hasanacitta) is another name for Hasituppāda, the rootless functional citta responsible for an Arahant's smile.
TERM_DAI_THIEN_38_M15: Mahākusala citta heads the group of 24 sense-sphere beautiful cittas (wholesome, resultant and functional) analysed together in the combination tables of mental factors.
TERM_THIEN_TAM_35_M15: Mahaggatacitta denotes the 27 exalted (fine-material and immaterial sphere) cittas considered together in the combination tables of mental factors.
TERM_SIEU_THE_36_M15: Lokuttaracitta denotes the supramundane path and fruition cittas considered together in the combination tables of mental factors.
TERM_PUGGALA_M16: A person (Puggala) is a conventional designation for a particular continuity of the five aggregates, classified in the Abhidhamma by which cittas can and cannot arise in it.
TERM_PHAM_THANH_M16: The classification of persons (Puggala-bheda) divides all beings into twelve types defined by their rootedness and, for noble ones, their stage of awakening.
TERM_KHO_VO_NHAN_M16: The woeful-destiny rootless person (Ahetuka puggala, duggati) is a being whose rebirth-linking consciousness is an unwholesome-resultant rootless citta, born in one of the four woeful states.
TERM_LAC_VO_NHAN_M16: The happy-destiny rootless person (Sugati ahetuka puggala) is a being whose rebirth-linking consciousness is a wholesome-resultant rootless citta — such as those born blind or deaf — reborn in a fortunate realm but without the wholesome roots.
TERM_SO_DAO_M16: The person on the path of stream-entry (Sotāpattimagga puggala) is one in whom the first path consciousness has just arisen, in the single mind-moment before its fruition.
TERM_TU_DAO_M16: The person on the path of Arahantship (Arahattamagga puggala) is one in whom the fourth and final path consciousness has just arisen, eradicating all remaining defilements.
TERM_BHUMI_M16: A plane of existence (Bhūmi) is one of the 31 realms into which beings can be reborn, grouped into the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere and the immaterial sphere.
TERM_NGU_TINH_CU_M16: The Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsā) are five fine-material realms reserved exclusively for non-returners, who attain Arahantship there without being reborn elsewhere.
TERM_DAI_DIA_NGUC_M16: The eight great hells (Aṭṭha mahāniraya) are the principal realms of the hell plane, the most intensely painful of the four woeful destinations.
TERM_JAMBU_M16: Jambudīpa is the southern continent of traditional cosmology, identified with the known inhabited world, where Buddhas appear.
TERM_MANUSSA_M16: Human beings (Manussā) occupy the human realm, a mixed destiny of the sense sphere where both wholesome and unwholesome kamma may be experienced and liberation is most readily pursued.
TERM_UPPATTIDEVA_M16: A generative deva (Uppattideva) is a being reborn by kammic generation into one of the six sense-sphere heavenly realms, as opposed to a deva merely by convention or by purification.
TERM_TUOI_THO_TROI_M16: A numeric lifespan value within the realms table, marking a figure rather than a named technical term.
TERM_SAC_GIOI_16_M16: The fine-material realms (Rūpāvacarabhūmi) are the sixteen Brahmā realms into which beings who have mastered the five fine-material jhānas are reborn.
TERM_VO_SAC_4_M16: The formless realms (Arūpabhūmi) are the four realms into which beings who have mastered the four immaterial jhānas are reborn, where there is mind without any materiality at all.
TERM_THUC_DUYEN_M17: 'Consciousness conditions mind-and-matter' (Viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpaṁ) is the formula for the third link of dependent origination, expressing how rebirth-consciousness gives rise to the mental and material aggregates of the new existence.
TERM_SAC_NGHIEP_TUC_SINH_M17: Kamma-born materiality (Kammaja-rūpa) arising together with rebirth-linking consciousness constitutes the physical half of mind-and-matter at the very start of a new life.
TERM_Y_NHAP_M17: The mind base (Manāyatana) is consciousness itself considered as the sixth sense base, the internal base that, together with mind-objects, conditions mental contact.
TERM_LUC_XUC_M17: Contact (Phassa) arising at each of the six bases is the condition, in this link of dependent origination, for the corresponding feeling to arise.
TERM_Y_THO_M17: Mental feeling (Manovedanā) is the feeling that arises specifically from mind-door contact, as opposed to the feelings arising through the five physical senses.
TERM_THO_DUYEN_AI_M17: 'Feeling conditions craving' (Vedanāpaccayā taṇhā) is the formula for the seventh link of dependent origination, showing how an unexamined feeling gives rise to craving for its continuation or cessation.
TERM_TU_THU_M17: The four kinds of clinging (Upādāna) are clinging to sensual pleasures, to views, to rules and rituals, and to a doctrine of self — the intensified form of craving.
TERM_NGHIEP_HUU_M17: Kamma-process becoming (Kammabhava) is the kamma-producing side of the link of becoming — the volitional activity that will generate a new existence.
TERM_SANH_HUU_M17: Rebirth-process becoming (Upapattibhava) is the resultant side of the link of becoming — the new existence and its aggregates actually produced by kamma-process becoming.
TERM_29_TAM_M17: Kamma-process becoming (Kammabhava) is the kamma-producing side of the link of becoming — the volitional activity that will generate a new existence.
TERM_BON_CACH_SINH_M17: The four modes of birth (Jāti, fourfold) are birth from an egg, from a womb, from moisture, and spontaneous birth, covering every way a being can come into a new existence.
TERM_SAUU_BI_KHO_UU_NAO_M17: Sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief and despair (Soka, Parideva, Dukkha, Domanassa, Upāyāsa) are the forms of suffering the texts list as flowing from ageing and death, completing the chain of dependent origination.
TERM_BA_THOI_M17: The three periods (Addhā) divide the twelve links across past, present and future lives: two links in the past, eight in the present, two in the future.
TERM_20_HANH_TUONG_M17: The twenty modes (Visākāra) break the twelve links down into five past causes, five present results, five present causes and five future results.
